title: Midpoint: The Valley Remembers

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Fifteenth Saying: A place remembers the hands that measured it.*

The mill yard smelled of wet slate and drying hay, a sharp, clean scent that cut through the damp chill of the Unmade. Isla stood before the gathered villagers, her boots still caked with the grey mud of the Pale, and tried to project an authority that she felt only in the soles of her shoes. The group was small: Old Perrin, leaning on his stick with the quiet dignity of a man who had outlived his own map; Wynne, the schoolmistress, whose eyes were sharp enough to cut paper; and the miller, a broad man with flour in his beard, who looked at Isla’s instruments as if they were a new breed of livestock.

"We can give you hands," the miller said, his voice rough with disuse. "We have ladders for the tower. We have water for the thirsty. But we will not give you time. Midsummer is close, and the river does not wait for paperwork."

Isla adjusted the strap of her satchel, feeling the solid, familiar pull of the sightglass against her hip. "I am not here to promise you a map," she said. "I am here to measure what is there. If the numbers hold, the land will stay. If they do not, I will tell you that too. I will not draw a line until I know it is true."

Perrin nodded slowly. He looked at her with a gaze that felt less like judgment and more like recognition, as if he were seeing a reflection of someone he had known long ago. "Hester said the same thing," he murmured, though it was too quiet for anyone else to hear. "She believed that a line must be earned, not just drawn. The hand was honest. The Guild was not."

Wynne stepped forward, her arms crossed. "Then show us the work. Show us the math. We have been waiting forty-four years for someone to explain why we disappeared. Do not waste this chance on polite silence."

Isla opened her field-book, the pages crisp and white in the dim light of the yard. "I will start tomorrow at dawn," she said. "But I need your help. I need you to hold still, to listen, and to trust the numbers over the hope. Can you do that?"

The miller grunted. "My wife holds a staff better than a sword. You have your surveyors."

Isla closed the book. The silence that followed was not empty; it was full of anticipation, heavy and thick as the fog that had finally lifted from the valley floor. She looked at the bell tower, its stone face weathered and silent, and felt a sudden, terrifying lightness in her chest. The Guild’s expectations, the pressure of the deadline, the shadow of her ancestor’s name, all of it seemed to recede, replaced by the simple, solid fact of the ground beneath her feet.
pages.image: In a wet stone mill yard at dusk, Isla Corrin, a sixteen-year-old with light-brown skin and auburn hair in a high knot, stands with a field-book open, addressing a small group of villagers including an old man with a white beard and a broad miller with flour in his beard.

pages.text:
Dawn broke in shades of pewter and pale gold, the light falling in long, thin stripes across the mill yard. The survey began not with a shout, but with a click. Isla set the tripod on the packed earth, the legs splayed wide, and leveled the sightglass until the bubble centered perfectly in the glass tube. It was a small, mechanical sound, but it felt like a key turning in a lock.

Wynne moved to the first position, holding the staff with a steadiness that surprised Isla. "I taught geometry for twenty years," she said, not looking up. "I know what a right angle looks like. I also know what a liar looks like." She adjusted the staff, her fingers tightening on the wood, and held it motionless while Isla read the angle.

Mags was already moving, carrying a bucket of water to the schoolmistress, who had forgotten to eat her breakfast. "Porridge," Mags said, handing over the cup. "It is oat and honey. It will fix your headache and your attitude. What does your village eat?"

Wynne took the cup, surprised. "We have the river fish and the orchard apples. But your porridge... it has a solidity to it. Like it is trying to hold the day together."

"I have been told it could hold up a bridge," Mags said, smiling. "I am trying to make it strong enough to hold up a surveyor."

Joss was by the mill-race, talking to the miller. They were examining the wooden sluice gate, pointing at the grain of the wood, discussing the flow of the water. Joss’s hands were quick, tracing the lines of the timber, and the miller nodded, his face softening into a look of professional respect. It was a quiet exchange, but Isla could see it: two people who understood structure, who knew that a bridge, a race, and a survey were all just different ways of making the world stand still.

The work was rhythmic. Isla read, Mags recorded, Wynne held. The numbers flowed onto the page, a steady stream of figures that felt, for the first time, like a conversation rather than a demand. Isla felt her shoulders loosen, the tension in her neck easing as the rhythm took hold. She was not alone in the numbers. She was part of a machine, a precise, human machine that was building something real.
pages.image: In the early morning light, Wynne holds a wooden surveying staff steady while Isla Corrin, in her mustard coat, looks through a brass sightglass on a tripod, Mags Okoro stands nearby holding a bucket of water, and Joss Harrowgate talks to a miller by a wooden water channel.

pages.text:
Three days later, inside the stone church of Ennis Vale, Isla found the mark. She had been digging through the local deeds, a dusty chest full of parchment that smelled of dried lavender and neglect, when Old Perrin led her to the back wall, near the altar. There, set flush into the ancient mortar, was a small bronze disc, no larger than a coin, with a tiny cross etched in the center.

"This is where Hester put her first station," Perrin said, his hand hovering over the metal without touching it. "She called it the Heart of the Vale. She said it was the one point that could not move."

Isla knelt, her knees protesting against the cold flagstones. She took out her steel tape, her fingers steady despite the chill, and extended it. The disc was smooth and unyielding under her thumb. She measured the distance from the disc to the corner of the altar, then to the window frame, and finally to the base of the pulpit. Three measurements. Three checks.

She pulled out her field-book and began to calculate. The numbers were familiar, but they did not fit. They were right, internally consistent, yet they did not match the baseline she had established from the Salt Flat. The discrepancy was small, only a few inches, but it was there, persistent and undeniable. It sat in the exact direction of the error she had found in Vell, the same tiny offset that had haunted her since the beginning of the commission.

She looked up at Perrin, who was watching her with a stillness that felt heavier than any physical load. "The numbers do not agree with my baseline," she said, tapping the page with a pencil. "But they agree with my great-grandmother’s work. Which means the error is not in the measurement. It is in the reference."

Perrin smiled, a thin, sad expression that crinkled the corners of his eyes. "The Guild’s benchmark in Vell is off. By a hair. Hester knew it. She did not trust their center. She trusted her own hands. And her hands were true."

Isla closed the book. The realization settled into her bones, solid and cold, like water seeping into a crack in a dam. It was not a mistake. It was a correction. Her great-grandmother had been right all along. The land had not drifted because of a surveyor’s error. It had drifted because the world had been measured from a lie.
pages.image: Isla Corrin kneels on a cold stone church floor, holding a steel tape measure against a small bronze disc embedded in the wall, while Old Perrin Ashdown, a tiny man in a patched green coat, watches her with a gentle, knowing smile.

pages.text:
Sera Quillon arrived at the edge of the orchard as the sun began to dip below the hills. She stood there, her plum-purple coat crisp against the tattered leaves of the old apple trees, her silver rule tucked neatly into her breast pocket. She had followed them, Isla knew. She had always followed, but this time she did not look like a rival. She looked like a student.

Isla did not turn around immediately. She was still writing, her hand moving quickly, the chalk squeaking softly against the slate. She could feel Sera’s presence, a cool, sharp pressure behind her shoulders. It was the feeling of a line that had not yet been checked, a tension that demanded resolution.

"You are working hard," Sera said, her voice flat and precise. "But you are missing the point."

Isla stopped. She turned slowly, her hair falling out of its knot, a single strand sticking to her cheek. "And what is the point, Miss Quillon?"

Sera stepped into the light, her face pale and serious. "You are trying to fix a valley. But a valley is not a shape. It is a part of a whole. You cannot seal this sheet without closing the traverse across the entire Unmade. You need to tie this place back to the network. Otherwise, it will just... float. Again."

Isla felt the air leave her lungs in a slow, controlled release. It was the truth, cold and sharp as a blade. Sera was right. The survey of Ennis Vale was beautiful, but it was isolated. It was a fragment, a single note in a chord that had not yet been struck. To make it real, to make it hold, they needed to connect it to everything else.

"That is impossible," Isla said, her voice dropping low, stripped of all ornament. "There are thirty-one days left. We have not even finished the northern ridge."

Sera shrugged, a small, elegant gesture. "Then you had better be quick. Or you had better be right. One of those two things is going to save you."

Isla looked at the orchard, at the trees that had waited forty-four years for a name. She looked at Sera, at the cold certainty in her eyes. And for the first time, she felt the scale of the task not as a burden, but as a challenge. A clear, sharp, defined challenge.
pages.image: Sera Quillon, a girl with a sleek black bob and a plum-purple velvet coat, stands at the edge of an old apple orchard at sunset looking down at Isla Corrin who kneels in the grass writing on a slate with chalk; only these two young women, no other figures.

pages.text:
The silence that followed was not empty. It was full of potential, a held breath that stretched across the valley, connecting the mill yard to the Salt Flat, the church to the Pale. Isla looked at the field-book, at the numbers that now made sense, and she felt a strange, quiet strength settling into her limbs. It was not the frantic energy of the last few days, but a deep, solid calm, like the water in the mill-race after a storm.

"We do it," Isla said. "We survey the whole Unmade. Not just the valley. The ridge, the gorge, the flat. All of it. We tie it all together."

Mags looked up from her porridge. "That is a lot of walking."

"Yes," Isla said. "But it is the right amount. It is the honest amount."

Joss nodded, his face set in a line of determination. "I can build the bridge. I can hold the structure. I just need the numbers."

Sera stepped forward, her silver rule catching the last of the light. "I will read the angles. I am faster than you. And I will check your work. Not to criticize. To ensure it holds."

Isla looked at them. Mags, with her iron pot and her steady hands. Joss, with his rope and his quiet strength. Sera, with her speed and her sharp eyes. And beyond them, the miller, the schoolmistress, the old man with the white beard. They were not just a team. They were a network. A web of trust and skill and truth, stretching out into the loose, drifting land.

Isla picked up her chalk. Her hand was steady. It had been steady for a long time now, but this time, it felt different. It felt like a promise. She looked out at the Unmade, the blank sheet that was waiting to be filled, and she felt, for the first time, that she was ready to draw the line.

The wind picked up, rustling the leaves of the orchard, carrying the sound of the river, the click of the tripod, the soft scratch of chalk on slate. It was a symphony of work, of creation, of truth. And Isla Corrin, the apprentice, the surveyor, the girl with the steady hand, was ready to play her part.
pages.image: Isla Corrin stands in the fading light of the orchard, holding a piece of chalk, surrounded by Mags Okoro, Joss Harrowgate, and Sera Quillon, all looking out toward the vast, hazy landscape of the Unmade with expressions of focused determination.
